stories.headline: Mistral Large 4 (“le Chonk”) previews a 1-trillion-parameter open-weight MoE, with 49B active and weights due end of month
stories.why_read: AI Top Story: the biggest thread on HN by far (~1,850 points / ~1,100 comments). It’s a European open-weight frontier model trained on Nvidia Grace Blackwell, and it makes an unusually blunt case on cyber capability versus refusals.
body: Mistral opened a public preview API for Mistral Large 4 on 6 October. It’s a natively multimodal model with 1 trillion total parameters and 49 billion active. Mistral says it was trained from scratch on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in the company’s own European datacenters, and the preview runs on that same hardware. Weights are promised by the end of the month. Until then the model is being red-teamed with cybersecurity leaders, vetted partners and state authorities. More than 160 languages went into training, including every official EU language.

The cyber section is the headline. Mistral says ML4 ranks in the top five on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index and scores 82% on a reproduce-then-patch-a-real-vulnerability test, the highest of any model. It argues that Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra score near zero on that test because they refuse it. On coding it reports 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1 and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. It also placed second of five in a blind Surge AI human eval, ahead of Kimi K3. These are vendor numbers for now. Once the weights are out, anyone, including teams self-hosting for security work, can check them.

stories.headline: SpaceX is reportedly lining up $40B of debt to buy Nvidia chips for its Colossus AI data centers
stories.why_read: Second Top Story, and it’s about compute: Anand RT’d the Bloomberg-sourced scoop (5,500+ likes), and X News says it would be one of the largest debt deals yet aimed at AI growth.
body: Per Bloomberg, via The Kobeissi Letter’s post that Anand reposted, SpaceX is in talks with banks and investors to raise about $40 billion of debt to buy Nvidia chips amid “insatiable demand” among AI developers. The rough split is $10 billion in bank loans and $30 billion in investment-grade bonds. X News adds that Apollo Global Management is leading. It says the money is for Nvidia hardware in the Colossus data centers, with plans to double a fleet of hundreds of thousands of chips by December.

The talks are described as early-stage and, if they succeed, expected to close in 2027. One investor joked that SpaceX’s two-page memo, with space photos and an arrow pointing to “data centers somewhere in the universe,” was a head-scratcher for approval committees. It follows Tuesday’s Diff items on SpaceX’s 10 GW compute plans and Wall Street’s $60B Anthropic TPU package. AI compute is now being funded the way railroads and telecom networks were, with very large debt.

stories.headline: OpenAI publishes a batch of new math results from an internal frontier model, with Lean proofs, compute estimates and reasoning summaries
stories.why_read: Featured: #3 on HN with ~970 points and ~930 comments. The interesting part is how they released it as much as what it found, with advice from IAS and proofs checkable in Lean.
body: OpenAI says it is releasing “a broad range of new mathematical results” produced by an unreleased internal frontier model. They’re published in a GitHub repository with protocols for paper revisions and citations, not as a press splash. The company says it consulted the Institute for Advanced Study’s independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence on best practices. Many of the proofs come with Lean formalizations, so a computer can check them, and more are promised as they’re completed.

The repo also includes 10 summaries of the model’s reasoning, statistics on how many problems were attempted, and compute estimates in ChatGPT Pro terms. OpenAI says the average result took roughly three hours of Pro thinking. It plans to fund workshops and conferences on understanding AI-produced results and is “working to responsibly release” the model. Given the size of the HN thread, how mathematicians judge novelty and exposition matters as much as the theorems.

stories.headline: Watch the first operational Starlink V3 satellites float out of Starship’s payload bay
stories.why_read: Featured: Anand bookmarked Sawyer Merritt’s post about the footage, which Sawyer calls “one of the best shots they’ve ever gotten.” It’s the moment Starship starts doing the job it was built for.
body: SpaceX released onboard video of the first operational Starlink V3 satellites deploying from Starship, and Sawyer Merritt’s post on it is in Anand’s bookmarks. X News’s summary of the reaction says the satellites came from Starship’s 14th test flight, the first to reach orbit. It counts 26 V3 satellites deployed smoothly, each with about 10 times the capacity of earlier Starlink models, and notes viewers saying the footage looks almost exactly like SpaceX’s renders.

The same summary ties it to SpaceX’s talk at the International Astronautical Congress. Michael Nicolls said Starlink now dodges collisions daily across 11,000+ satellites serving 13 million customers. V3 is the payload Starship was sized for, so a clean deployment video is the visible part of a much bigger capacity jump.

stories.headline: Grok Bot becomes a model router: Claude Opus 5.5 for agents, Midjourney for images, Suno for music, and users like it
stories.why_read: Featured: Anand RT’d both Theo (“Grok Bot is actually really good”) and Mike Pat’s “one interface to rule them all” write-up. Using the best model for the job, rather than only your own, matters for his fleet.
body: X News reports that Grok Bot, SpaceXAI’s agent for coding, email and web work, now routes jobs to whichever backend is strongest for the task, preferring the best result over in-house Grok models. That means Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 for agent work, Midjourney for images and Suno for music. Team member lauren confirmed bots will use Opus 5.5 and spawn agents from the available models. Users mostly praised the pragmatism. Some asked about privacy when data is shared with third-party models.

Two posts Anand reposted show how people use it. Theo’s “Bad news guys: Grok Bot is actually really good 🙃” passed 1.8M impressions. Mike Pat (@mikepat711) published an X article, “Grok Bot: The One Interface to Rule Them All,” on driving Claude, Grok Build and Muse Spark subscriptions from Grok Bots acting as the “prime orchestrator and front door.” That is the same multi-bot pattern Anand already runs.

stories.headline: Meta and Sierra announce the Personal Agent Protocol, an open standard for how your agent talks to businesses
stories.why_read: Featured: Anand RT’d Bret Taylor’s announcement (2,000+ bookmarks). If personal agents are going to shop, book and resolve support tickets, someone has to define the handshake, and Shopify, Stripe and Walmart are on board.
body: Bret Taylor announced the Personal Agent Protocol, an open standard that Meta and Sierra are developing with industry partners Genesys, @instinct, @RocketOTD, Shopify, Stripe and Walmart. Its goal is to define how personal agents interact with businesses. That’s the agent-to-merchant counterpart to the tool and agent-to-agent protocols developers already use. The partner list covers commerce, payments, contact centers and the biggest retailer, which suggests the target is everyday transactions rather than demos.

How reliable those agents are is the open question. X News also covered micro1’s new PersonalAgentBench, a living leaderboard that scores agents including Gemini Spark, Instinct, Muse and Grok Bot on real tasks from real user accounts, for both completion and trustworthiness. Early results have Gemini Spark ahead at 60–70%, helped by tight integration with Gmail and Flights. A standard handshake plus a public trust score is how this category moves past demos.

stories.headline: GitHub says Git activity more than doubled in a year, to 473.3B events a month, and it’s rebuilding Git infrastructure for agent scale
stories.why_read: Featured: Anand RT’d it. A developer-platform architect will see the numbers immediately: agents are now a load profile, and GitHub is replacing the core while it keeps running.
body: In a post Anand reposted, GitHub says Git activity more than doubled between September 2025 and August 2026, reaching 473.3 billion events per month. The accompanying article, “Building Git infrastructure for agent-scale development,” says GitHub is rebuilding its Git infrastructure while the service keeps running, as a foundation for agent-scale software development. In other words, it’s a live migration of the system everyone depends on.

For anyone running enterprise CI/CD this is a familiar curve. Fleets of coding agents open branches, push and fetch far more often than humans do, and clone and push traffic grows with them. Today’s Gergely Orosz keynote makes the same point from the people side: most code is now written by agents running in parallel. GitHub’s numbers are the infrastructure version of that story.

stories.headline: Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2026 to Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai, who showed how chemistry can pick one mirror image
stories.why_read: Featured: #2 on HN this morning, a day after Tuesday’s IceCube physics prize. It answers a century-old puzzle about why life is single-handed, and it matters for drug manufacture.
body: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the 2026 chemistry prize on 7 October to Henri B. Kagan (Université Paris-Sud) and Kenso Soai (Tokyo University of Science) “for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis.” Many molecules, including amino acids, come in two mirror-image forms, but life uses only one. That property is called homochirality. Ordinary lab reactions tend to produce equal amounts of both forms.

Kagan took the first step in 1986 with a way to manipulate reactions that produced a bigger excess of one mirror image than anyone thought possible. Soai designed a reaction in 1995 that could in principle be homochiral, and in 2003 he showed one that formed only one of the two mirror images. Apart from life itself, nobody had done that before. Committee chair Heiner Linke called the reactions “spectacular,” and the academy says they have been decisive for chemists designing how pharmaceuticals are made.
authors: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences

stories.headline: Strands Decider 2B: an open-source “decision model” that picks answers in tens of milliseconds, plus an SRE pipeline built on one
stories.why_read: HN (~200 points): a new class of small models that only choose between options. They’re fast, calibrated and local, and that makes them useful plumbing for agent workflows.
body: The Strands team released Strands Decider 2B, a 2-billion-parameter decision model. Models in this class don’t generate text. They choose from supplied options or give a score, along with a reliability estimate. Strands took a Qwen3.5-2B base, removed the LM head and attached a small pointer head of just over a million parameters that scores each option. The base is fine-tuned with a rank-16 LoRA. It runs on a local CPU or GPU and answers in tens of milliseconds. The team says it ranks 3rd of 33 in its size class on JevBench’s public set for accuracy and Brier-score calibration. Code, weights, training data and scripts are all open.

SREGym shows what this looks like in practice. It built a Kubernetes diagnosis pipeline driven by TypeSafe AI’s Jev decision model with no LLM agent. Code collects cluster evidence and Jev chooses the likely root cause and the supporting observations. Across 21 SREGym-Lite faults the pipeline passed 80 of 105 diagnoses (76.2%), with a median diagnosis time of 14.6 seconds.

stories.headline: OpenAI’s Decisions API enters public beta: typed yes/no, choice and rubric answers about 10x faster than Responses
stories.why_read: HN (~320 points): OpenAI is betting on the same idea as Strands Decider today. Classification and routing calls get their own fast endpoint.
body: OpenAI’s new Decisions API takes text, images or both and returns typed answers: the probability that a condition is true, a choice from a fixed set, or a score against a rubric. The docs say it’s about 10x faster than the Responses API. It’s aimed at classifying content, routing requests and prioritizing work. It’s in public beta with GA expected “in the coming weeks,” and gpt-6-luna is currently the only model, served from a dedicated POST /v1/decisions endpoint.

The enterprise details are there from day one: Zero Data Retention and HIPAA eligibility for qualifying customers, and data residency in the US and Europe. Many agent systems still spend frontier-model tokens on yes/no gates, so a cheaper, faster decision primitive is likely to end up in a lot of pipelines.

stories.headline: EmbeddingGemma 2: a 740M-parameter open model that embeds text, code, images, audio and video in one space on-device
stories.why_read: HN (~345 points): an Apache-2.0 embedder small enough for a phone, with a big jump on code retrieval, which is useful for local coding-agent search.
body: Google DeepMind released EmbeddingGemma 2, built on the Gemma 4 architecture under Apache 2.0. It maps combinations of text, code, images, video and audio into one embedding space. The full model is 740M parameters, but it’s modular: about 270M for text-only, with optional 170M vision and 300M audio encoders. Context is 8K tokens, 4x the first version. That’s enough for about 5.5 minutes of audio or 29 images in one input.

Code is the standout. MTEB Code rises from 68.76 to 78.68, which Google pitches for local codebase indexing and coding-agent retrieval. Matryoshka truncation lets vectors shrink from 768 dimensions down to 128, for up to 6x storage savings. Quantized on a Pixel 11 Pro, it needs about 191MB of RAM for text-only and about 567MB for the full multimodal model. The first EmbeddingGemma passed 20 million downloads.

stories.headline: Armin Ronacher on Codemode: why Pi 1.0 lets agents script tool calls in a sandboxed JavaScript on the harness
stories.why_read: HN: a clear mental model, “brains vs hands,” from the person who argued for scripts over MCP. Now he explains why Pi added MCP support through Codemode.
body: Armin Ronacher, who wrote “Code Is All You Need,” explains why Pi 1.0 now supports MCP through Codemode. Bash composes well, but only for things that run as programs in the execution environment. Some tools have to live in the trusted harness: reading an image into the model, spawning and coordinating sub-agents. He calls the harness the brain and the execution environment, often sandboxed and on a different filesystem, the hands.

Codemode lets the model write JavaScript that issues tool calls on the harness side, so intermediate results don’t pass through the context window. In Pi it runs in QuickJS inside a WASM runtime with no network, no filesystem, no timers and limited RAM. All it can do is call more tools. Agents can run calls concurrently, process large structured outputs (a plain bash tool call puts only the trailing 2,000 lines into context), and keep state between calls. He credits Cloudflare with the name.

stories.headline: openTPU: an AI accelerator designed by AI agents, from RTL to compiler, running Qwen3 and Gemma 4 on a Kintex-7 FPGA card
stories.why_read: HN (~300 points / ~350 comments): asks whether agents can build the chip that runs their own inference, and the repo is meant to be read end to end.
body: openTPU applies the lessons of the auto-arch-tournament project to AI accelerators. It asks how far AI agents can get at hardware design, and whether they can build the chip that runs their own inference. One monorepo, at 1,423 commits, holds the SystemVerilog design, the ISA, a bit-exact simulator, a kernel language and compiler, a profiler and the host software for a real PCIe card. That card is an Inspur YPCB-00338 with a Xilinx Kintex-7 xc7k480t and two DDR3 channels.

The README says ten modern models run with their real weights and the card produces exactly the same tokens as the simulator. Numbers are modest, as you’d expect from DDR3. LFM2.5-230M decodes at 85.8 tok/s on-device at 4-bit, and Qwen3-0.6B manages 21.6 tok/s at int8, while DRAM bandwidth use reaches the 80–90% range. The authors also pitch it as a learning project: “from a matmul in Python down to the wires.”

stories.headline: Cursor lets you run your desktop agents from your phone, and power users love its Projects coordinator
stories.why_read: Anand RT’d both. Checking in on agents from an iPhone and having a coordinator agent delegate work is very close to how he runs his own bot fleet.
body: Cursor announced that you can now control agents running on your computer from your phone: check in, reply or start new tasks from the Cursor iOS app. The launch post drew 1,800+ likes and 200+ replies. It’s a small feature that changes the routine. Long-running agent work no longer means sitting at a desk.

@chsrbrts, in a second post Anand reposted, says he “can’t overstate” how much he likes Cursor’s Projects feature. He describes it as working with a highly engaged product-engineering lead, the coordinator agent, who hands out work and context to engineers and PMs (the sub-agents), so he no longer has to decide when to spin up a new agent himself.

stories.headline: “Product engineering” vs “factory engineering”: improve the agents that improve the product, and keep caring past day two
stories.why_read: Anand RT’d three short posts that together describe where engineering effort is moving: tending the agent setup, curating skills, and staying with a project.
body: Ben Holmes (@BHolmesDev) splits engineering work into product engineering, which improves the product, and factory engineering, which improves the agents that improve the product. Lauren (@poteto) calls the second kind “gardening.” The post has 440+ bookmarks, more than its like count, which usually means people are saving it to use. Wes Bos’s reposted line is shorter: “the only moat left is caring about your project past two days” (4,700+ likes).

The third post is the factory itself. @0xblacklight lists “skills I can’t live without”: /show-me from @dexhorthy, /bro from @backnotprop, a custom /effect-program-design based on @kitlangton’s, and /rpi:create-research bundled with @humanlayer_dev. It has 1,300+ bookmarks. Skills files are turning into the shared, reusable part of agent-driven engineering.

stories.headline: Gergely Orosz’s LDX3 keynote, “The state of the tech industry in 2026”: almost nobody hand-writes code, and code review has become theater
stories.why_read: Anand RT’d it. A 29-minute snapshot for engineering leaders, drawing on visits to OpenAI, Anthropic and Ramp and on unpublished data from GitHub, Factory and Linear.
body: Gergely Orosz gave this keynote to 2,000+ engineering leaders at LDX3 New York. It splits into what changed, what broke, what stayed the same, and what’s next. What changed: practically nobody writes code by hand anymore, working with 5–10 parallel agents is common, and the IDE is fading. He quotes Claude Code creator Boris Cherny on running five terminal tabs of Claude plus 5–10 more on the web. Martin Fowler gets the line “Nothing has hit with the magnitude of AI.”

What broke: assumptions about code output, code reviews that “became theatrical,” and falling quality and reliability. What hasn’t changed: teams and planning still matter, and non-engineers still mostly aren’t shipping code. What’s next: cloud coding agents and harnesses, engineers who stop reading the code, and a new kind of AI infrastructure. The full video is free. Slides are for paid subscribers.

stories.headline: State of Devs 2026: about two thirds of developers feel less motivated and more cynical, and 62% have burned out at some point
stories.why_read: HN (~190 points): the human-cost counterpart to the agent-productivity story, from 5,463 respondents.
body: Devographics surveyed 5,463 developers between 5 July and 5 September 2026. In the overview, Miranda Heath of the Software Stewardship Lab says it “is an uncertain time to be a developer.” Nearly half of respondents had experienced job insecurity and insufficient wages. A quarter had been laid off at some point, nearly 1 in 10 within the past nine months, and more than a quarter expect to need a career change within five years.

This was the first year the survey asked about mental state. Around two thirds reported reduced motivation and growing cynicism about their work or industry, and around half reported trouble focusing, procrastination and feeling drained. 62% said they had experienced burnout at some point in their career, the same as last year. A small number wrote in “AI fatigue” on their own.

stories.headline: Andy Bechtolsheim: AI has made high-speed optics demand about 10x bigger in five years, and it’s “the very beginning”
stories.why_read: Anand RT’d it. Networking is the part of AI infrastructure a Cisco engineer knows best, and Arista’s co-founder is saying the optics curve has barely started.
body: In a clip shared by @firesidealpha, Arista co-founder Andy Bechtolsheim says AI has driven “this incredible increase in demand for high-speed optics.” He puts it at roughly 10 times bigger over five years and says the industry is only at the “very beginning.” The post reached more than 1.2 million impressions.

It fits today’s lead. GPU fleets in the hundreds of thousands, like the Colossus build-out SpaceX is reportedly financing, need huge amounts of switching and optical interconnect, and memory and bandwidth are becoming the constraints that matter. GPUs get the headlines, but optics and networking are a big part of the bill.

stories.headline: A million-mile trucker who called the Tesla Semi “stupid” drives one fully loaded: “This industry is going to be changed”
stories.why_read: Anand RT’d it. A skeptic changing his mind on camera, and honest about the charging trade-off, is more persuasive than a spec sheet.
body: Chansoo’s video post, which Anand reposted, follows a million-mile trucker who once called the Tesla Semi “stupid” as he drives one fully loaded. His verdict: “This industry is going to be changed.” By his account the truck lost only 1 mph climbing a 7% grade. He is candid about charging being a trade-off, and then does the fleet math out loud: “Why would I buy a diesel truck…”

The post has nearly 5,000 likes and almost 1,500 bookmarks. Class 8 electrification will be decided by owner-operators and fleet managers who run these numbers, not by launch events, which is why driver conversions like this one matter.

stories.headline: FSD in owners’ words: “the most unbelievable technology,” “let FSD do its thing,” and a hit-and-run caught on every camera
stories.why_read: Anand RT’d all three, a snapshot of what living with a Tesla looks like this week.
body: Tesla’s own account reposted an owner’s reaction from a Model Y L on FSD (Supervised): “This is the most unbelievable technology I have ever experienced in a car.” It passed 1.1 million impressions. Dirty Tesla quoted a clip from another driver and wrote: “This is why I increasingly just let FSD do its thing even if I think it’s being dumb (because I am usually dumb).”

The third post shows a different benefit. Mike Pat says his Model Y Launch Series was rear-ended in traffic and the other driver fled. Because he drives a Tesla, he has HD footage of the impact from the rear camera and of the driver leaving from the front camera. The cameras FSD relies on also work as a dashcam. The post drew 3,000+ likes and 200+ replies.

stories.headline: Drone footage shows about 200 Cybercabs lined up in a Houston lot, with roughly 300 more in Dallas
stories.why_read: X News: the Texas Cybercab inventory keeps growing in plain sight. Monday’s Diff had Dallas, and now Houston is in the picture.
body: X News says new drone video from Houston shows roughly 190 to 200 gold, steering-wheel-free Cybercabs parked in neat rows. Spotter S.E. Robinson, Jr. counted 15 of them charging while others drove in and out on test runs. Similar clusters of about 300 appear in Dallas. Austin, Anand’s city, already has public Cybercab service along with hundreds of daily driverless sightings.

The summary cites Texas registrations listing 169 Cybercabs as of early October, with Giga Texas building inventory for unsupervised rides. It also says no expansion timelines for Houston or Dallas have been set. Treat the lots as a staging signal, not a launch date.

stories.headline: At IAC, SpaceX sketches Starmind (up to a million AI satellites in laser-linked clusters) and Starlink for the Moon and Mars
stories.why_read: X News: the Kardashev-scale version of the AI compute race, presented at the International Astronautical Congress in Antalya.
body: SpaceX’s Michael Nicolls laid out an interplanetary Starlink roadmap at the International Astronautical Congress in Antalya, Turkey, according to X News. It starts with a lunar constellation, extends to Mars, and reuses the laser links already flying in Earth’s Starlink network, which has more than 11,000 satellites and 13 million customers. He also stressed space safety, urging operators to share trajectories so close approaches can be avoided.

The bigger idea is Starmind: up to one million AI satellites in sun-synchronous orbits. Clusters of about 10 would be linked by 10 terabits of bandwidth to run large models on constant sunlight, avoiding the land, grid and cooling limits of ground data centers. One summary puts initial launches as early as late 2027, pending FCC approval. Concerns about crowded orbits are already part of the discussion.

stories.headline: FCC approves SpaceX to launch 15,000 direct-to-cell satellites for voice, text and data on unmodified phones
stories.why_read: X News: a large expansion of cell service from orbit, with deployment milestones running to 2035.
body: On 6 October the FCC approved SpaceX to launch and operate 15,000 low-Earth-orbit satellites for direct-to-cell service, covering voice, text and data on ordinary unmodified phones in the U.S. and beyond, X News reports. The system uses spectrum from EchoStar and a patented signal-timing technique meant to keep performance steady across narrow beams, with deployment milestones set through 2035.

Starship’s lift capacity makes the plan practical, and it puts SpaceX in direct competition with carriers on coverage gaps. Open questions remain about indoor use and the orbital safety of yet another very large constellation.

stories.headline: SpaceX’s $250M Gigabay at Starbase is designed for up to 1,000 Starships a year, reviving the debate over demand
stories.why_read: X News: the factory side of Starship, and a fair argument about whether launch supply can create its own demand.
body: X News says SpaceX is building a $250 million Gigabay facility at Starbase, Texas, laid out in work cells with cranes to assemble and refurbish up to 1,000 Starships a year for satellite deployments and deep-space missions. Enthusiasts are already listing uses: AI satellite networks, orbital data centers, refueling depots, lunar outposts and asteroid mining.

Skeptics ask whether demand can absorb that much launch capacity without flooding the market. Supporters argue that cheaper launches will create new industries the way cheap bandwidth did. Read together with Starmind and the $40B chip-debt story, the factory is being sized for SpaceX’s own AI ambitions as much as for outside customers.

stories.headline: A chart on X: pre-training fell from 67% of frontier-lab compute in early 2024 to 7% now, as RL and inference take over
stories.why_read: X News: a quick way to see why benchmark gains are uneven and why hardware priorities are shifting toward memory speed.
body: A chart going around X tracks how frontier labs split their compute. Pre-training goes from 67% in early 2024 to just 7% by late 2026, while post-training and reinforcement learning now take 55% and inference holds at about 38%, according to X News. The usual explanation is the data wall. Ilya Sutskever warned in late 2024 that pre-training as we know it would end because there is only one internet.

Spending on RL for math, coding and agent tasks fits several other stories today: OpenAI’s math results, Mistral’s coding numbers, and decision models built for agent workflows. The summary notes the shift favors memory speed over capacity in hardware. It also notes skeptics such as Toby Ord question how compute-efficient RL really is, while total compute keeps growing fast.

stories.headline: Mustafa Suleyman amplifies Daron Acemoglu: in 10 years, only 5% of what humans do will be replaced by AI
stories.why_read: Anand bookmarked it. A deliberately low estimate from a Nobel economist, shared by a frontier-lab executive, is a useful counterweight to today’s State of Devs anxiety.
body: Mustafa Suleyman’s post, which Anand bookmarked, sums up an X article on Daron Acemoglu’s prediction from issue 1 of The Humanist Review: “AI won’t take your job anytime soon. In 10 yrs, only 5% of what humans do will be replaced by AI.” Acemoglu has long been a prominent skeptic of fast AI-driven automation and productivity gains.

It’s notable that the head of an AI lab is the one sharing the low number. It sits alongside today’s other signals: developers reporting burnout and job insecurity, the online turn from AI excitement to doubt that X News describes, and Gergely’s claim that almost nobody writes code by hand. A small share of tasks replaced can still change a great deal of work.

stories.headline: “Waymo was born too early”: a 12-minute video argues HD maps were a brilliant crutch, and that FSD shows the intelligence was missing
stories.why_read: Anand bookmarked it. It states the vision-versus-maps argument clearly, from an FSD-sympathetic point of view.
body: Genma (@nymbusjp) argues in a 12-minute video that Waymo’s HD map was “a brilliant crutch: centimeter-perfect, hand-checked, roof-lidar-dependent… and impossible to scale.” The thesis is that relying on the map shows the driving intelligence is missing, and that this is “why FSD drives anywhere.” Anand bookmarked the post.

It’s an advocacy piece, so read it with Tuesday’s Austin data in mind: Tesla robotaxis briefly outnumbered Waymo sightings on traffic cams, while a Cybercab looped a parking lot for 14 minutes. Waymo still has the much larger national footprint. Whether general driving skill beats pre-mapped precision will be settled at scale, which is what both companies are now trying.

stories.headline: Attackers hijacked the .gh, .sl and .as ccTLDs and got counterfeit TLS certificates for Google and other big brands
stories.why_read: HN: an attack on the trust chain that every CA validation check relies on. Google’s advice for domain owners (watch CT logs, publish strict CAA records) is directly actionable.
body: Google says attackers took control of the .gh, .sl and .as country-code top-level domains, rewrote authoritative DNS and nameserver delegations for selected domains in those namespaces, and used that control to pass CAs’ automated domain-control validation. That got them unauthorized certificates for “several Google domains” and “several leading global brands and widely used online services.” Chrome now blocks every certificate Google identified, and the ones for Google properties were revoked. Google says no domain owner’s infrastructure was breached and the CAs followed the rules, as Ars Technica reports.

Google’s warning is that browser blocking “should not be relied on.” It can’t guarantee it found every affected domain, and Chrome’s interventions don’t protect non-Chrome users. The guidance: monitor Certificate Transparency logs for unexpected issuance, and publish restrictive CAA records so attackers can’t reuse cached validation after DNS control is restored. Ars compares it to the 2011 DigiNotar breach.

stories.headline: A Pi-hole-class DNS ad-blocker on a $2 ESP32-C3: 537k domains as 40-bit hashes in flash, no PSRAM
stories.why_read: HN (~120 points): a classic close-to-the-metal trick. Don’t load the blocklist into RAM, binary-search hashes in flash.
body: esp32-c3-adblock is a DNS sinkhole with a web dashboard that runs on a $2 ESP32-C3 with no PSRAM. Most ESP32 blockers load domain strings into RAM, which requires an ~$8 board with PSRAM. This one hashes each domain, plus its parent suffixes, with 40-bit FNV-1a, stores the sorted hashes in flash and binary-searches them. Blocked queries get 0.0.0.0, and misses are forwarded upstream.

The numbers in the README: 140,000+ domains fit in about 0.7MB of flash, lookups take about 10ms including WiFi round trip, and RAM use is around 50KB. The author explains why 40 bits: by the birthday bound you get roughly zero collisions at 141k domains and about one at 537k, whereas 32 bits would mean around 7 collisions at 250k. On a 16MB ESP32-S3 the same approach holds around 2.7 million domains.

stories.headline: A font rebuilt from photographs of real Commodore 64 keycaps, PETSCII graphics included
stories.why_read: #1 on HN this morning, and a nice bit of nostalgia for someone who has been at a Unix prompt since 1996.
body: C64 Keyboard is a typeface reconstructed from photographs of classic Commodore 64 keycaps, with cleaned-up shapes and consistent proportions. It comes as TTF, OTF and a webfont. It includes uppercase letters, numbers, punctuation, arrows and £, selected accented characters including Hungarian ones, f1–f12 function-key labels and the classic C64 key legends.

It also includes all 63 PETSCII graphic front legends as smooth geometric reconstructions. A preview page lets you click to insert them, with Commodore+key and Shift+key legends laid out as on the real keyboard. It recreates the printed keycaps, not the screen bitmap font, which is why lowercase input shows as uppercase.
